steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Procedure" section of an encyclopedia article on Article 6ter of the Paris Convention: how emblems get notified and protected, and how other parties can object.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Notifying WIPO of emblems
- Publication in the Article 6ter Express Database
- Date of publication and time periods
- Obligations of countries
- Objections and grounds
- Effect of an objection

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Notifying WIPO
  - who: state party to Paris Convention, or IGO with one or more member States party to it
  - notifies WIPO of emblems/marks it wants protected
- Publication
  - WIPO communicates to all member countries
  - semi-annual electronic publication, Article 6ter Express Database, WIPO website
  - each record: category of sign, requesting entity (State or IGO), in English and French
  - reproduction of sign + relevant info (contact details, classification of figurative elements, etc.)
- Date of publication
  - in the record; counts as date of receipt by any party bound to apply 6ter
  - time periods of Article 6ter(4) and (6) calculated from it
- Obligations
  - countries must prevent use/registration of trademarks including or imitating the emblems
- Objections
  - within twelve months after publication, any bound party may object to a particular sign (Article 6ter(4))
  - example grounds: not a symbol of sovereignty of communicating State; not a hallmark for products; pertains to a lower entity; earlier trademark right already protected in the jurisdiction
  - objection info (objecting State, date) shown in sign's bibliographical data in the database
- Effect
  - objecting party not obliged to apply 6ter to that sign
  - protection in non-objecting parties not affected

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
To get protection under Article 6ter, a state that is party to the Paris Convention, or an intergovernmental organization that has one or more member States party to the Paris Convention, has to notify WIPO of the emblems or marks that it wants to protect.

WIPO then passes this information on to all of the member countries. It does this with a semi-annual electronic publication, which is in the Article 6ter Express Database on the WIPO website.

Each record in the database has the category of the sign and the entity (State or IGO) that asked for it to be communicated, and this is published in English and French. There is also a reproduction of the sign and other relevant information, like contact details, the classification of the figurative elements, etc.

The record also mentions the date of publication. This date is taken to be the date that the communication was received by any party that is bound to apply Article 6ter. So the time periods in Article 6ter(4) and (6) of the Paris Convention are calculated from the date of publication.

- countries must then take measures against use/registration of trademarks that include or imitate the emblems
- objections: within twelve months of publication, any party bound to apply 6ter can object to a sign (Article 6ter(4))
- example grounds:
  - not a symbol of sovereignty of the communicating State
  - not a hallmark for products
  - pertains to a lower entity
  - earlier trademark right already protected in the jurisdiction
- objection info (objecting State, date) goes into the sign's bibliographical data in the database
- objecting party doesn't have to apply 6ter to the sign; protection in the other parties not affected

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
To get protection under Article 6ter, a state that is party to the Paris Convention, or an intergovernmental organization that has one or more member States party to the Paris Convention, has to notify WIPO of the emblems or marks that it wants to protect.

WIPO then passes this information on to all of the member countries. It does this with a semi-annual electronic publication, which is in the Article 6ter Express Database on the WIPO website.

Each record in the database has the category of the sign and the entity (State or IGO) that asked for it to be communicated, and this is published in English and French. There is also a reproduction of the sign and other relevant information, like contact details, the classification of the figurative elements, etc.

The record also mentions the date of publication. This date is taken to be the date that the communication was received by any party that is bound to apply Article 6ter. So the time periods in Article 6ter(4) and (6) of the Paris Convention are calculated from the date of publication.

Then the countries have to take measures to prevent trademarks that include or imitate these emblems from being used or registered.

But after the signs are published, any party bound to apply Article 6ter can object to the protection of a particular sign. It has twelve months from the date of publication to do this (Article 6ter(4)).

Some of the grounds that objections have been based on are:

the sign is not a symbol of sovereignty of the communicating State

the sign does not constitute a hallmark for products

the sign pertains to a lower entity

an earlier trademark right is already protected in the jurisdiction

The information about objections (the name of the objecting State and the date of the objection) is shown in the bibliographical data of the sign in the Article 6ter Express Database.

A party that objected does not have to apply Article 6ter to that sign. The protection of the sign in the parties that did not object is not affected.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The procedure for invoking Article 6ter protection involves a state party to the Paris Convention, or an intergovernmental organization of which one or more member States are party to the Paris Convention, notifying WIPO of the emblems or marks it wants to protect.[1,2]

WIPO then communicates this information to all member countries through a semi-annual electronic publication in the Article 6ter Express Database on the WIPO website.[3]

Under each record of the database, the category of the sign and the entity (State or IGO) that requested its communication are published in English and French, along with a reproduction of the sign and any relevant information (contact details, classification of the figurative elements, etc.).

The date of publication, which is also mentioned in the record, is considered to be the date of receipt of the communication by any party bound to apply Article 6ter. The time periods provided for in Article 6ter(4) and (6) of the Paris Convention are therefore calculated from that date of publication.

The countries must then take measures to prevent the use or registration of trademarks that include or imitate these emblems.

However, after the signs are published, any party bound to apply Article 6ter may, within twelve months of the date of publication, issue an objection to the protection of a particular sign (Article 6ter(4)).[4]

Examples of grounds on which objections have been based include:

the sign is not a symbol of sovereignty of the communicating State

the sign does not constitute a hallmark for products

the sign pertains to a lower entity

an earlier trademark right is already protected in the jurisdiction

Information on objections (the name of the objecting State and the date of the objection) is reflected in the bibliographical data of the sign in the Article 6ter Express Database.

A party that issued an objection is not obliged to apply Article 6ter to the sign concerned. Protection of the sign in the parties that did not issue an objection is not affected.[2]

References:
[1] WTO intellectual property (TRIPS) — notifications: state emblems. www.wto.org. https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/trips_e/trips_notif7_sixter_e.htm
[2] General Information on Article 6ter - article-6ter - WIPO Liferay DXP. article-6ter. https://www.wipo.int/web/article-6ter/general_info
[3] New signs notified under Article 6ter of the Paris Convention. GOV.UK. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/new-signs-notified-under-article-6ter-of-the-paris-convention/new-signs-notified-under-article-6ter-of-the-paris-convention
[4] Protection systems for official designations: Article 6ter of Paris Convention and U.S. laws protecting national trademarks and certification marks. https://hki.umm.ac.id/files/file/MATERI%20Webinar%20USPTO%20-%20Art6terTMs-ASEANRegion-09-23-2020.pdf
